lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Backtesting a strategy usually means walking through candles one at a time. nova-backtest does something smarter: it works on whole columns of data at once, and still finds exactly where each trade ends.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Start from the top. What is it?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A Python library for backtesting crypto trading strategies, published on PyPI. It downloads historical candles from eight exchanges, including Binance, Bybit and OKX, runs a strategy over many pairs at once and reports statistics. This repository is a fork of the NovaLabs project.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: How do you write a strategy?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: You subclass one class and fill three methods on a table of candles. The first adds indicators. The second marks entry signals, with a take profit, a stop loss and a position size. The third sets the exit signal.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: In how it finds the exit. A signal on one candle is filled at the next candle's open, so the strategy can't trade on a price it just used to decide. Then, for each candle ahead, the code builds a column saying when the stop or the target was touched, and takes the earliest exit among the stop, the target, a maximum holding time and an exit signal.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Can you walk through a trade?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Sure. Say the strategy buys at one hundred with a five percent target and stop, so the target is one oh five and the stop ninety-five. Two candles later nothing happens. On the third, the high reaches one oh five and the low stays above the stop. The trade exits at one oh five, a plus five percent move.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: They're charged on the way in and on the way out, at the exchange's maker rate. On Binance, at point oh two percent, that trade costs about four hundredths on a notional of a hundred, leaving a profit near four point nine six.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And with many pairs trading together?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The trades from every pair are merged and sorted by exit time, and anything that would open beyond the maximum number of positions is dropped, because a real account couldn't have taken it. Each position gets a share of the bankroll based on leverage.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What comes out at the end?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A CSV of per-pair statistics, a JSON file of overall statistics and a Plotly equity graph. The written page has the full flow diagram and the code's formulas.
